thread.title: UPDATE: Tax overhaul is a credit negative for tech sector, S&P says

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: Tax overhaul is a credit negative for tech sector, S&P says
text:
By Wallace Witkowski, MarketWatch
Tech 'may never look the same again,' S&P warns
The overhaul of the U.S. tax law may be good for tech companies, many of which have kept billions of dollars overseas because of tax rates, but in the long run, it may weaken the credit profile of the sector.
In a Thursday report, S&P Global Ratings warned investors that "the technology sector may never look the same again," now that the U.S. tax overhaul will allow for tech giants to bring back billions of dollars from overseas coffers. While viewed as an overall positive, it could also result in more fast and loose financial policies that could damage creditworthiness in the sector. Earlier in the week, Morgan Stanley downgraded the tech sector (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/morgan-stanleys-wilson-warns-investors-not-to-buy-the-dip-2018-02-05) on signs of weakening earnings.
S&P said it believes "the overall industry credit profile will weaken over time, largely because of the potential for more aggressive financial policies in response to greater access to overseas cash."
Resulting lower cash balances will result in weaker credit metrics ultimately, S&P said, and those aggressive financial policies appear to be key. S&P noted:
"If an issuer adopts a more aggressive financial policy than we expect after repatriation, likely through additional share repurchases, its credit metrics could deteriorate based upon our policy of netting surplus cash against debt, potentially leading to rating or outlook revisions. Generally, we will not deduct surplus cash from debt if a company is (1) owned by a financial sponsor as defined in our criteria, or (2) has a business risk profile at the lower end of the scale (i.e., weak or vulnerable as described in our criteria)."
S&P points to Apple Inc.'s (AAPL) recent announcement that it plans to go from having $163 billion in cash to becoming "net-cash neutral over time," (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-has-163-billion-to-burn-and-tim-cook-plans-to-spend-it-2018-02-01) and said the tech giant could be a trend setter for the industry.
See also:Tax overhaul will have a limited effect on U.S. economy, Moody's says (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/tax-overhaul-will-have-a-limited-effect-on-us-economy-moodys-says-2018-01-25)
"We anticipate that other large cash holders will also announce enhanced shareholder returns over time," S&P said. Topping that list along with Apple is the only AAA-rated tech issue Microsoft Corp. (MSFT), along with Alphabet Inc.(GOOGL)(GOOGL), Cisco Systems Inc.(CSCO) and Oracle Corp.(ORCL)
Then, there are those companies who have as much about as much debt as they have cash to repatriate. Should those companies use the repatriated cash to return to shareholders and still hold on to the debt, that could be harmful to their rating.
Read: Tax overhaul will lead to as many ratings downgrades as upgrades, says S&P (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/tax-overhaul-will-lead-to-as-many-ratings-downgrades-as-upgrades-says-sp-2018-02-08)
S&P noted:
Unlike issuers with large net cash positions, we believe those that have both high cash and debt balances face potential credit risks because they may choose to use substantial portions of now-accessible foreign cash for shareholder returns. These issuers, some of which have modest net cash positions or are in net debt positions, will have to manage a delicate balance between equity holders and debtholders. Depletion of cash, if not offset by some debt reduction, can raise leverage by our calculation and lead us to consider a downgrade.
S&P used Oracle as an example, pointing out that while it has $72 billion in cash, about 35% of its market cap, it also has $61 billion in debt so its net cash is relatively low, at about 5% of market cap. Other companies in this boat include Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.(HPE), Western Digital Corp.(WDC) and Intel Corp.(INTC), S&P said.
"We believe companies with these types of balance sheets will have to clarify their financial policies to both equity and bond investors over the coming quarters as cash comes back on shore," according to S&P.
Tech companies that have seen their stocks underperform over the past year or so are particularly vulnerable, because there's more incentive to return money to shareholders to boost stock prices. S&P said:
We are very attentive to the repatriation-related earnings call comments from issuers whose share prices have underperformed the overall market during the past year. Issuers with meaningful cash balances offshore are likely engaged in deep board-level discussions to finalize their capital allocation strategies and we have already heard from some management commenting about "return of excess capital" to shareholders. We believe that management of companies whose share prices have lagged the market will feel greater pressure to appease the shareholders through aggressive share repurchases or risky acquisitions.
One example S&P used was Juniper Networks Inc.(JNPR). Over the past 12 months, shares of Juniper have declined 8%, compared with the 15% gain in the S&P 500 index and the 22% rise in the Nasdaq Composite Index .
On the other hand, companies like Nvidia Corp.(NVDA) and Micron Technology Inc.(MU), which are up 90% and 70%, respectively, over the past 12 months, will have a lot more flexibility with the timing a size of shareholder returns and will likely be better able to balance stock and bondholder needs, S&P said.
Read now:The tax bill is making the fourth-quarter earnings season a muddle (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-tax-bill-is-making-the-fourth-quarter-earnings-season-a-muddle-2018-02-02)
-Wallace Witkowski;
